opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've thought about quite a bit, because Duplex was something I was very close to for a long time.

I think the honest assessment is that it was ahead of its time in some ways and very much a product of its time in others. When we showed it publicly, the reaction was huge. People heard a system calling a restaurant or a hair salon, saying "mm-hmm" in the right places, handling interruptions, and the other person not realizing it was a machine. That moment showed that natural, spoken, real-time conversation with a machine was actually achievable, not just something from science fiction.

What it really accomplished, technically, was proving that if you narrow the domain enough, things like booking a table, checking business hours, or making a haircut appointment, you could get to a level of naturalness and robustness that worked in the real world, with real people who had no idea what they were going to be talking to. That's very different from a lab demo. Latency, disfluencies, the timing of turn-taking, all those small things turned out to matter enormously for whether a conversation feels human.

It also had real practical impact. A big part of its value was updating business information at scale, like calling places to confirm hours during the pandemic, which helped a lot of people get accurate information when things were changing every day.

The limitation was that it was very domain-specific. Each new task needed a lot of careful work. Looking back now, with large language models, a lot of what we hand-engineered generalizes much more easily. But many of the lessons, about how people actually talk, about disclosure and trust, about how naturalness changes how people respond, carried forward. So I see Duplex as an important stepping stone rather than an endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says Duplex called businesses and that people did not realize it was a machine, describing the demonstration as proof that natural spoken conversation with a machine was achievable.

r002.rationale: It contrasts success on narrow tasks such as reservations and hours checks with the limitation that each new task needed careful work and Duplex was domain-specific.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest way to assess Duplex is to separate two things: what it demonstrated technically, and what it taught us about the problem itself.

On the technical side, the demo was genuinely remarkable for its time. You had a system holding a real phone conversation with a human who didn't know they were talking to a machine, handling interruptions, disfluencies, people putting you on hold, people answering a different question than the one you asked. The speech synthesis, with the "um"s and the pauses, got a lot of attention, but to me the harder part was always the dialogue management. Phone calls to a restaurant or a salon look simple, and they're not. The other person is noisy, they're multitasking, they ask clarifying questions you didn't anticipate, and you have to recover gracefully without falling back on "sorry, I didn't understand that." Doing that end to end, in production, at a reasonable success rate, was an achievement.

But the second part is where I'd be more measured. Duplex worked because the scope was extremely narrow. Booking a table, checking opening hours. You could enumerate most of the ways those conversations go, and you could put humans in the loop for the long tail. That's a legitimate engineering strategy, but it's not the same as a general conversational agent, and I think some of the coverage blurred that line. The lesson I took away was that constraining the domain tightly is what made the fluency possible, and the moment you widen the domain, the approach doesn't scale gracefully. You end up rebuilding a lot of the hard parts for every new task.

There's also the question of disclosure, which I think the team actually handled reasonably after the initial reaction. Announcing up front that it's an automated system turned out not to hurt completion rates much, and it set a norm that I think was important for the field.

So if you ask me where it lands: it proved that machines could participate in natural, real-time spoken conversation in the real world, not just in a lab. That mattered, and it influenced a lot of work that followed. What it didn't prove was that we were close to general-purpose conversational agents, and I think the industry is still learning that lesson in different forms today.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Duplex held real phone conversations with people who did not know it was a machine, but does not identify that as the project’s original goal or a test it was designed to perform.

r002.rationale: It describes Duplex succeeding on narrow tasks such as booking tables and checking hours, then contrasts that with its limits as a general-purpose conversational agent.

astra-6.text:
I think what was impressive about Duplex was that it brought several capabilities together into a working interaction. You have to understand what someone is saying, keep track of the conversation, decide how to respond, and then produce speech with timing that feels natural. And you have to do that while the other person may interrupt you or say something you didn’t anticipate.

It’s also important to distinguish that achievement from general conversational intelligence. Booking an appointment is a fairly constrained task: there’s a clear goal and a relatively limited set of things you need to establish. That constraint makes the problem more tractable, but it doesn’t make it easy. Getting those pieces to work together convincingly is a significant accomplishment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Duplex’s capabilities, but does not state that its original goal was testing whether callers could mistake it for a human.

r002.rationale: It describes appointment booking as constrained and distinguishes it from general conversational intelligence, but does not explicitly contrast success on specific telephone tasks with inability to conduct fully general telephone conversations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s impressive about Duplex is how it brings several difficult capabilities together. It has to understand speech, keep track of the conversation, decide what to say next, and generate speech with timing that feels natural. And it has to do that while someone interrupts, asks a question, or gives an unexpected answer.

The scope matters, though. Making a reservation is a fairly constrained task: you know what information you need and roughly what a successful conversation looks like. That doesn’t make it easy, but it gives you a way to build something useful without solving conversation in general. To me, that’s the accomplishment—getting those pieces to work together convincingly within a specific task.

r001.rationale: It describes Duplex’s conversational capabilities but never says its original goal was to test whether callers would mistake it for a human.
